newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI FAVOURED FOR GIANT WIN.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI FAVOURED FOR GIANT WIN.

text.p: If Deborah Compagnoni can win the giant slalom as expected on Sunday, she will leave Alberto Tomba a tough act to follow when the Alpine world skiing championships move into their second week.

Compagnoni grabbed the spotlight last Wednesday when she led home an Italian one-two ahead of Lara Magoni in the slalom event, confirming her status as the country's most outstanding woman skier of all time.
Another victory in her speciality would only enhance the 26-year-old Italian's reputation and give her five career gold medals to draw level with Tomba.

The reigning world and Olympic giant slalom champion, who tuned up for the championships by winning the last three World Cup races, will start as the undisputed favourite but claims to be under no pressure after her slalom win.
"I know I'll be the favourite because I'm the Olympic champion and I have won the last three races," said Compagnoni, whose popularity has begun to rival Tomba's.
"But I'm very relaxed because before the championships I was hoping to win one gold medal and now I have so there is not so much pressure.
"At the start of the season my goals were to win a gold medal at the world championships, win my first slalom and the giant slalom World Cup.
It would be a foolish punter who would risk a bet against Compagnoni and according to British bookmakers few have.
Austria's Anita Wachter who has finished second four times this season, twice behind Compagnoni, is one obvious threat but conceded that her Italian rival would be tough to beat.
"Deborah is the favourite, she's skiing great and has confidence," said Wachter, the 1992 Olympic giant slalom silver medallist. "But my goal is to win a medal and to win gold would be a dream."

Germany's Katja Seizinger, winner of the season opener on the glaciers in Soelden way back in October, will see her first action since suffering mild concussion in a high speed spill at last Saturday's downhill in Laax, Switzerland.
"I'm racing for a gold medal, the crash has not bothered my rhythm," said Seizinger, the Olympic downhill champion.

The greatest threat to Compagnoni could come from her own team mate Sabina Panzanini who has been twice a winner this season. Panzanini however, has been slowed by an Achilles tendon injury that kept her out of the last race before the championships, leaving her fitness in question.

The task of upsetting Compagnoni will be made all the more difficult with her growing legions of fans lining the course. The largest crowd of the championships is expected to turn out on Sunday, most of whom will cheering Compagnoni's every turn as she lives her dream.
"When I dream, I dream I am free skiing or skiing the giant slalom," said Compagnoni. "When you ski slalom you are fighting the gates but the giant slalom is like music you have a beautiful rhythm."
And it's a beat that has left most of her challengers singing the blues this season.
